meta.note: Documented history of this cloth starts at Lirey in the 1350s. Everything before that is either a separate documented object (Mandylion, Sudarium) whose link to this cloth is hypothesized, or legend. Years before AD are negative only where a numeric year is needed; here all events are AD.

events.title: Crucifixion and burial of Jesus
events.text: The Gospels say Joseph of Arimathea wrapped the body in a linen cloth (sindon) and laid it in a rock tomb. John mentions linen cloths and a separate face cloth. Any link to this Shroud is a hypothesis.

events.title: Eusebius records the Abgar letters, no image
events.text: Eusebius preserves a letter between King Abgar of Edessa and Jesus. No image is mentioned. The image enters the legend later.

events.title: Pilgrim Egeria sees letters, not an image
events.text: Egeria visits Edessa and reports the Abgar letters but no image of Christ.

events.title: First mention of an Edessa image
events.text: Evagrius Scholasticus credits a miraculous image with saving Edessa from the Persian siege of 544. Ian Wilson later proposed this face image was the Shroud folded so only the face showed.

events.title: Sudarium said to leave Jerusalem
events.text: Legend says the face cloth now at Oviedo left Jerusalem ahead of the Persian invasion. The story is recorded centuries later by Bishop Pelagius, known as a forger.

events.title: Mandylion moved to Constantinople
events.text: The Image of Edessa is taken to Constantinople and placed in the Pharos chapel. The transfer is documented; that it was this Shroud is a hypothesis rejected by most historians.

events.title: Sudarium chest opened at Oviedo
events.text: Alfonso VI, his sister and El Cid open the chest holding the Sudarium. It is the earliest explicit record of that cloth.

events.title: Pray Codex drawing
events.text: A Hungarian manuscript shows Christ's burial with crossed hands, no thumbs, and a cloth with L-shaped circles like the Shroud's old burn holes. Critics read the object as a decorated tombstone.

events.title: Robert de Clari's figured shroud
events.text: A French crusader writes that a shroud showing the figure of the Lord was raised every Friday at Blachernae in Constantinople. No other source confirms it.

events.title: Sack of Constantinople
events.text: Crusaders loot the city's relics. Some historians suggest a burial cloth disappeared then and later reached France. This is a hypothesis.

sources.label: Wikipedia: History of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: Templar initiate kisses a linen image
events.text: Arnaut Sabbatier testified he was shown a long linen cloth with a bearded man's image at his Templar initiation. Barbara Frale proposed in 2009 that this was the Shroud.

events.title: Lirey church founded
events.text: Knight Geoffroi de Charny founds a collegiate church at Lirey in Champagne. The official Turin site calls this the start of the first certain evidence.

sources.label: Wikipedia: History of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: First showings at Lirey
events.text: Canon Robert de Caillac begins exhibiting the cloth at Lirey. Pilgrim badges bearing the Charny and Vergy arms, one now in the Musee de Cluny, show front and back images of a body.

events.title: Geoffroi de Charny dies at Poitiers
events.text: The founder of Lirey is killed at the Battle of Poitiers. He never left a written account of how he got the cloth.

events.title: Oresme calls a Champagne shroud a fake
events.text: Theologian Nicole Oresme cites a church in Champagne claiming the Lord's shroud as a clear case of clerical fraud. The passage was identified by Nicolas Sarzeaud in 2025.

events.title: Bishop d'Arcis memorandum
events.text: The Bishop of Troyes writes to Antipope Clement VII that the cloth is cunningly painted and that an artist confessed to an earlier bishop. The surviving texts are unsigned drafts.

sources.label: Wikipedia: History of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: Clement VII allows display as a 'representation'
events.text: The antipope permits showings only if it is announced as a figure or representation, with no candles, incense or guard of honour.

sources.label: Wikipedia: History of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: Removed from Lirey
events.text: During the Hundred Years War, Marguerite de Charny takes the cloth from Lirey for safekeeping. The canons later sue for its return.

events.title: Passes to the House of Savoy
events.text: Marguerite de Charny transfers the cloth to Duke Louis of Savoy. It stays Savoy property until 1983.

events.title: Julius II approves a feast
events.text: Pope Julius II approves a liturgical feast of the Holy Shroud for Savoy on 4 May, treating it as a relic.

events.title: Fire at Chambery
events.text: Fire in the Sainte-Chapelle of Chambery melts part of the silver reliquary. Molten metal burns through the folded cloth, leaving a symmetrical pattern of holes and scorches.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Conservation-restoration of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: Poor Clare nuns patch the holes
events.text: The nuns sew patches over the burn holes and add a Holland cloth backing.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Conservation-restoration of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: Calvin attacks it
events.text: John Calvin's Treatise on Relics mocks the shroud shown at Nice as a fake.

sources.label: Wikipedia: History of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: Moved to Turin
events.text: Duke Emmanuel Philibert brings the cloth to Turin, the occasion being a pilgrimage by Carlo Borromeo. It has stayed in Turin since, apart from wartime removals.

events.title: Guarini chapel and Valfre repairs
events.text: The cloth is placed in Guarino Guarini's chapel, where it rests until 1993. Sebastian Valfre reinforces it.

sources.label: Wikipedia: History of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: Princess Clotilde repairs it
events.text: Clotilde of Savoy repairs the cloth. It is displayed from 24 to 27 April 1868 for the wedding of the future Umberto I.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Conservation-restoration of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: Secondo Pia's negative
events.text: Amateur photographer Secondo Pia finds that his negative plate shows a clear, positive-looking human figure. Modern scientific interest begins here.

events.title: Vignon studies the image geometry
events.text: Paul Vignon studies how a cloth over a body would distort an image and notes the image looks like an orthogonal projection, a point raised again by Moraes in 2025.

events.title: Enrie's photographs
events.text: Professional photographer Giuseppe Enrie confirms Pia's result with sharper plates. Enrie's images were used in later 3D and 2025 modelling work.

events.title: First scientific commission
events.text: The Archbishop of Turin appoints a commission, kept confidential at first, to examine the cloth's condition.

sources.label: Wikipedia: History of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: First TV exposition and first samples
events.text: The cloth is shown live on television. Threads are cut for study, including those Gilbert Raes examined, and Max Frei takes tape samples for pollen.

events.title: VP-8 analyser shows 3D information
events.text: Using a VP-8 Image Analyzer at Sandia, John Jackson and Eric Jumper find an Enrie photo gives a coherent relief. This leads to the formation of STURP.

events.title: Public exposition and STURP examination
events.text: About 3 million people view the cloth. Afterwards the STURP team studies it for five days around the clock, taking photos, spectra, X-ray fluorescence and sticky-tape samples.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Shroud of Turin Research Project

events.title: McCrone says it is paint
events.text: Walter McCrone reports red ochre and vermilion in a collagen binder on the 1978 tapes and concludes it is a 14th-century painting. He leaves STURP in 1980 and publishes his case in Accounts of Chemical Research in 1990.

events.title: STURP papers in Applied Optics
events.text: STURP publishes spectral, infrared, UV and blood results, including Heller and Adler's 'Blood on the Shroud of Turin'.

events.title: STURP final summary
events.text: STURP concludes the image is not paint and not the product of an artist, the stains contain hemoglobin, and how the image formed remains a mystery. Heller and Adler publish their chemical study.

events.title: Given to the Holy See
events.text: Ownership passes from the House of Savoy to the Holy See. A papal custodian, the Archbishop of Turin, looks after it.

sources.label: Wikipedia: History of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: Image intensity versus distance paper
events.text: Jackson, Jumper and Ercoline publish in Applied Optics that image shading correlates with cloth-to-body distance (r squared 0.60 from 13 points).

events.title: Radiocarbon sample cut
events.text: In the cathedral sacristy, Giovanni Riggi cuts a strip from one corner. Pieces go to Arizona, Oxford and Zurich, with three control cloths. Part is kept in reserve.

events.title: Nature publishes AD 1260-1390
events.text: Damon and colleagues from the three labs report a 95% range of AD 1260-1390 and call it conclusive evidence of a medieval date. Cardinal Ballestrero announced the official range on behalf of the Church.

events.title: Sudarium of Oviedo radiocarbon dated
events.text: Arizona, Toronto and Madrid date the Sudarium to between the 6th and 9th centuries, most likely around AD 700.

events.title: Cathedral fire
events.text: Fire breaks out in the Guarini chapel. Firefighter Mario Trematore smashes the bulletproof case with a sledgehammer and the cloth is carried out unharmed.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Conservation-restoration of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: John Paul II: not a matter of faith
events.text: In Turin, the pope says the Church has no specific competence to rule on authenticity and entrusts the question to scientists, calling the Shroud a mirror of the Gospel.

sources.label: Vatican: John Paul II address, 24 May 1998

events.title: Great Jubilee exposition
events.text: The cloth is shown publicly for the Jubilee year.

sources.label: Wikipedia: History of the Shroud of Turin

events.title: Major restoration
events.text: Mechthild Flury-Lemberg's team removes the 30 patches of 1534 and the Holland backing, fits a new backing, and scans both sides. Some scholars criticise the work as damaging evidence.

events.title: Claimed faint image on the back
events.text: Fanti and Maggiolo report a faint face image on the reverse from 2002 photographs. Direct observers in 2002 reportedly saw none.

events.title: Rogers: the dated sample was different
events.text: Raymond Rogers argues in Thermochimica Acta that the radiocarbon area has cotton and a gum-dye coating and estimates the cloth at 1,300 to 3,000 years old from vanillin loss.

events.title: Oxford tests the carbon monoxide idea
events.text: Christopher Ramsey tests whether carbon monoxide could add young carbon to linen and finds no significant effect.

events.title: Garlaschelli's full-size replica
events.text: Chemist Luigi Garlaschelli shows a life-size cloth made by rubbing an acidic pigment over a volunteer and a bas-relief, then baking and washing. The paper appears in 2010.

events.title: ENEA ultraviolet laser studies
events.text: ENEA physicists colour linen with very short UV laser pulses and get thin, Shroud-like yellowing. They stress this does not show how the image was actually made.

events.title: Arizona re-examines a dated fragment
events.text: Freer-Waters and Jull find no dye or coating and only a few cotton fibres on a leftover Arizona fragment. The cloth is also shown publicly in 2010.

events.title: Statistics paper and Fanti's dating book
events.text: Riani and colleagues publish the spatial-trend analysis in Statistics and Computing. Fanti announces FT-IR, Raman and mechanical dates near the first century; the Archbishop of Turin says the material's origin is not certain.

events.title: Freeman's Easter-prop theory
events.text: Historian Charles Freeman argues in History Today that the cloth was a faded, once-painted prop for medieval Easter dramas.

events.title: Exposition and first DNA survey
events.text: The cloth is shown with Pope Francis's approval. Barcaccia and colleagues report plant and human DNA from many regions, adding that a medieval European origin is not excluded.

events.title: Raw radiocarbon data released
events.text: After a legal request, the British Museum releases the 1988 labs' raw data to researcher Tristan Casabianca.

events.title: Bloodstain pattern study
events.text: Borrini and Garlaschelli report in the Journal of Forensic Sciences that the blood flows imply inconsistent postures. A public exposition is held in August.

events.title: Raw data show heterogeneity
events.text: Casabianca and colleagues publish in Archaeometry that the raw data lack homogeneity and the 1988 procedure should be reconsidered, while not ruling out a medieval date.

events.title: Livestreamed exposition in lockdown
events.text: During the COVID-19 lockdown, the archdiocese shows the cloth by television and online. Pope Francis calls it an icon of the crucified, dead and risen Lord.

events.title: Two more statistical reanalyses
events.text: Walsh and Schwalbe, and Di Lazzaro and colleagues, publish that the shroud results are heterogeneous with a spatial trend and that the medieval conclusion should be reconsidered.

events.title: WAXS dating of one thread
events.text: De Caro and colleagues report in Heritage that one thread's cellulose ageing matches a Masada linen of AD 55-74, under assumed storage conditions.

events.title: Neutral review: date stands, retest needed
events.text: A review in Textiles concludes the evidence against the 1989 date is not enough to overturn it, image formation is still a mystery, and a second radiocarbon test is needed.

events.title: Digital Shroud for the Jubilee
events.text: Instead of a physical exposition, Cardinal Repole presents a life-size digital replica in a tent in Piazza Castello, Turin.

events.title: Moraes: a low relief fits better
events.text: Cicero Moraes publishes 3D draping simulations in Archaeometry suggesting a low-relief sculpture fits the image better than a body. The Turin centre CISS replies on 4 August that this is not new.

events.title: Oresme passage published
events.text: Nicolas Sarzeaud publishes the Oresme text in the Journal of Medieval History, the earliest known written rejection of the cloth.

events.title: Rebuttal to Moraes in Archaeometry
events.text: Casabianca, Marinelli and Piana publish a critique of Moraes's model in the same journal, citing modelling errors and ignored evidence.

events.title: Second Arizona fragment examined
events.text: Freer-Waters and Jull publish in Heritage Science on a leftover 1988 Arizona fragment. Press reports say they found no sign of a repair or foreign material.

events.title: Regression on the raw data
events.text: Riani, Atkinson, Corbellini and Di Lazzaro publish a reanalysis of the raw data in Statistical Methods and Applications, testing all 165,888 possible subsample layouts.

events.title: New examination of the Sudarium
events.text: EDICES and the University of Oviedo report the first non-invasive technical examination of the Sudarium since 2012.

events.title: DNA study of the 1978 samples
events.text: Barcaccia and colleagues report in Scientific Reports that the main human DNA matches the scientist who collected the samples, plus many plant, animal and microbial traces. Two reliquary threads date to the 1534 and 1694 repairs.

events.title: Blood and image order tested
events.text: Kelly Kearse shows that blood on acid-treated linen blocks later colouring, so 'no image under blood' does not fix the order of events.
